insight.title: Why Office Chairs Have That "Loud" Fabric
insight.subtitle: The rough, speckled upholstery in your cubicle is designed to hide stains and muffle the sounds of a busy workspace.
insight.notificationHook: Why office chairs are so scratchy

sections.text: Ever wonder why office chairs are almost always covered in that coarse, multi-colored, synthetic fabric? It isn’t for comfort or style; it’s a tactical choice made by facilities managers to keep the office looking clean.

The mottled, dark-flecked pattern is specifically engineered to camouflage everything from coffee spills to skin cells. By masking daily wear and tear, it prevents the office from looking neglected long before a replacement is needed.

Beyond the visuals, the thick, dense weave acts as an acoustic sponge. It absorbs ambient noise and chair-shifting creaks, preventing your workspace from sounding like a hollow, echoing chamber during a quiet afternoon.
A chair that hides your mess and swallows your silence.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain news of the day.

The Trump administration issued a rule to restrict China from accessing advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The rule targets five countries, including Malaysia and Thailand, where Chinese companies use data centers to train artificial intelligence models. Companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil must now apply for United States export licenses for the most advanced chips. The Commerce Department said the rule ensures existing restrictions cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements in third countries.

The European Union is imposing tariffs of up to 27.9 percent on cold-rolled flat steel products from India, Japan, Taiwan, Turkey and Vietnam. The European Commission said the products were being sold at unfairly low prices in the European Union. The anti-dumping duties will apply from November 17. The rates are set at 9.5 percent for Indian companies, 27.9 percent for Japanese steelmakers, and mostly 20.7 percent for Taiwanese producers. Vietnamese producers face a 16 percent duty rate, while Turkish steelmakers face duties ranging from 3.0 percent to 7.8 percent.

Turning to energy, average United States diesel prices dropped below $6 per gallon on Monday for the first time since September 10, according to AAA data.

Nvidia plans to work with IBM and the United States Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory on a quantum codesign platform. The three partners will use Nvidia DGX B200 systems alongside IBM quantum computers to research modular quantum computers, error correction and scientific applications. Fermilab will steer the work toward error correction and physics. Nvidia also released a new decoder called TCBP-JOBS that decodes up to 13,000 times faster than leading existing algorithms.

Urgent pleas for cash from poor nations at the COP31 talks in Turkey face a sluggish response from Western governments. Rich countries previously agreed to triple climate funding for poorer countries to $300 billion per year by 2035. Host country Turkey and lead negotiator Australia emphasized making previous pledges work rather than securing a new headline target. Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale told the conference that small island states remain in perpetual climate disaster recovery mode. The Solomon Islands pledged $400,000 from its own pocket, and the Bahamas committed $75 million to protect and restore its seagrass meadows.

A Vulcan rocket owned by United Launch Alliance failed mid-flight on Sunday shortly after liftoff from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The flight was the joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin's first mission failure and destroyed 40 satellites from Amazon’s Leo internet network. The rocket suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight after the separation of the second stage from the first-stage booster. United Launch Alliance stated that the cause was not immediately clear and that no specific data was available yet. The failure is expected to keep the rocket off the market for months.

Next, we look at whether Nvidia artificially boosted its earnings with suspect sales to China, according to questions raised by Scott Bessent.

Senator Maria Cantwell urged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China. Cantwell sent a letter to Lutnick on Sunday ahead of a meeting with Chinese leaders. Nvidia is a U.S. company that designs advanced AI chips. Cantwell said Lutnick failed to stop restricted chips from reaching Chinese companies. She pointed to potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons. She said their firm held one point two billion dollars in Nvidia stock. Former Nvidia leader Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Lutnick agreed to testify before the Senate banking committee in December. Lawmakers instructed officials to preserve all export documents by November seventeenth.

Next, Iran is facing natural gas shortages as winter approaches. The government forecast a winter deficit of about four hundred thirty million cubic meters per day. Strikes by the United States and Israel damaged six gas refineries on March eighteenth. The strikes knocked out twenty-eight percent of Iran's gas production capacity. Iran has since restored about one hundred million cubic meters per day of capacity. Full recovery of the lost capacity could extend into twenty twenty-eight, the government said. Gas accounts for seventy-three percent of Iran's total energy mix. Household gas consumption reached four hundred eighty million cubic meters per day. A spokesperson warned gas might be cut off across the country if consumption grows.

In health news, the Association of American Medical Colleges held its annual meeting in California. The group spent two years involved in health policy debates during President Trump's second term. Leaders spoke after Democrats won control of the House and Senate in midterm elections. Public policy officer Danielle Turnipseed said major health policy issues will not fade away. Group chief executive David Skorton noted that international graduates make up one quarter of practicing physicians. Skorton said public mistrust is fueled by times when organizations were not trustworthy. He said he believes that trust needs to be earned. A federal restriction blocking political control over research grant decisions ends on December eleventh.

Turning to international trade, farmers in the United Kingdom are pushing for a new trade deal. They want to ease border barriers with Europe. Reporter Charlie Angela spoke with a farmer in Sussex about the issue. The farmer hopes a proposed deal between the United Kingdom and Europe may ease trade barriers.

In business news, Blackstone acquired a majority stake in data center joint ventures with Amazon. The transaction is structured as a five billion dollar deal. The trust acquired a majority interest in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services.

Turning to finance, the United States dollar index reached a nineteen-month high on Monday. The index advanced for a fifth straight day to one hundred three point five two. It rose zero point one percent on Monday. Investors awaited comments from Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh about interest rates. Japan's economy contracted by an annualized zero point one percent in the third quarter. Forecasters had expected the Japanese economy to grow by zero point three percent. The yen strengthened zero point one percent to one hundred fifty-nine point five nine per dollar. Traders price an eighty-nine point seven percent chance of a rate hike in December.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Have you ever wondered why office chairs feature coarse, multi-colored fabric? Facilities managers choose this synthetic upholstery to keep offices looking clean. The dark, speckled pattern is engineered to camouflage coffee spills and skin cells. By masking daily wear, it stops furniture from looking neglected before replacement. Beyond appearance, the thick weave acts as an acoustic sponge. It absorbs background noise and chair creaks during quiet afternoons. This keeps your workspace from sounding like a hollow, echoing chamber. It is clever how one material hides daily mess while swallowing room noise. Next time you sit down, will you notice what your chair is doing?

Thank you for listening to this episode of the Sift Daily Briefing.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This is the full analysis of today’s top stories.

How can the United States stop China from getting the most powerful computer chips? The government is now forcing companies in five countries to get special permission before sending these chips to overseas data centers. For years, the U.S. has tried to keep its most advanced artificial intelligence technology out of China. Officials worry that if China uses these chips, they could build powerful intelligence models that threaten American security. Because of this, the U.S. previously banned companies like Nvidia from selling their best chips directly to Chinese firms. However, Chinese companies began using data centers in other countries to access the chips remotely. This allowed them to bypass the rules.

The situation changed when the Commerce Department realized that smugglers were finding ways to get these chips to China anyway. There was also a recent scandal involving a former executive at a company called Megaspeed. Reports alleged that she helped divert restricted chips to China, which led to the resignation of Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang. These events pushed the government to act.

On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Department released a new rule. It requires exporters to get a license before sending advanced AI chips to firms in Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. These countries were chosen because the U.S. sees a high risk that chips sent there could be illegally diverted to China. Companies must now do careful checks on their customers to ensure the chips are not being used to help China or other restricted nations. Nvidia, which holds about 90 percent of the market for these chips, saw its stock price fall about 1.6 percent after the announcement.

This is happening now because the U.S. is under pressure to close these loopholes before President Trump meets with President Xi in Shenzhen this week. Officials want to show they are serious about protecting sensitive technology.

Looking ahead, this could make it harder and more expensive for Chinese firms to train their AI models. We will have to watch if these new checks actually stop the smuggling, or if companies find yet another way around the rules.

Moving on, why is the European Union putting extra taxes on steel from five different countries? The EU decided to charge these countries more because it says they are selling their steel at unfairly low prices. The European steel industry has been struggling for some time. Companies in Europe say they cannot compete when steel from places like India, Japan, and Taiwan arrives at such cheap prices. They argue this puts European factories and thousands of jobs at risk. In 2025, a group called Eurofer asked the European Commission to investigate these low prices.

The investigation changed things by using a new method to judge pricing. Usually, the EU compares a country's export price to what they charge at home. But the Commission found what it calls "particular market situations" in India and Taiwan. In India, the EU claims government rules on iron ore costs made local prices artificial. In Taiwan, they say cheap Chinese steel flooded the market and pushed prices down. Because of this, the EU decided to ignore those local prices and set its own values to calculate the taxes.

Starting November 17, the EU will apply these new "anti-dumping" duties. Japan faces the highest tax at 27.9 percent. Vietnam will see a 16 percent tax, while India faces 9.5 percent. Turkey’s taxes range from 3 to 7.8 percent, and Taiwan’s rates are between 20.7 and 27 percent. This affects a market worth over 23 billion euros. These duties are intended to protect the 8,600 people employed in the EU's own steel production.

This is happening now because the Commission wants to show it can create new tools to fight trade practices it considers unfair. It sees this case as a way to set a standard for future trade disputes.

This could lead to higher costs for European companies that buy steel for cars, planes, and buildings. We should watch to see if these countries challenge the EU’s decision at the World Trade Organization.

Average diesel prices in the United States dropped below six dollars per gallon on Monday for the first time since September 10. This change follows a recent decline in oil prices. Diesel costs had previously risen sharply during the war involving Iran, which caused price increases throughout the economy.

Nvidia is now working with IBM and Fermilab on a new platform designed to help scientists build better quantum computers.

How can scientists build powerful quantum computers that do not make so many mistakes? Nvidia is teaming up with IBM and Fermilab to connect classical supercomputers directly to quantum hardware.

Quantum computers use quantum physics to process information in ways normal computers cannot. However, today's quantum processors constantly make errors while running calculations. These frequent errors limit how long and how complex calculations can be. To fix this, scientists use a method called error correction. This process spreads each piece of quantum data across multiple physical bits, called qubits. Next, a classical computer program called a decoder reads measurements to fix the errors. Fermilab is the Department of Energy's Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory. Fermilab has worked with Nvidia software before to design quantum systems. In September, Nvidia software cut a Fermilab design project from five months to three weeks. In October, Nvidia simulated a 104-qubit quantum computer on Germany's JUPITER supercomputer.

Nvidia announced a new partnership with IBM and Fermilab to build a quantum testing platform.

The three partners will link Nvidia DGX B200 systems with IBM quantum computers. These include machines running IBM's Nighthawk processor. Nvidia called Nighthawk the fastest quantum processor IBM has delivered. Researchers will use the system to build error-correction codes for high-energy and nuclear physics. Anna Grassellino from Fermilab described the project as a proposed platform. The partners did not provide a start date or a cost for the project. Nvidia also introduced a new decoder called TCBP-JOBS in its software library. Nvidia claimed it decodes up to 13,000 times faster than leading existing algorithms. The company said this cuts research computing time from 12 weeks down to 45 minutes. Additionally, IBM and Japan's RIKEN institute paired a quantum computer with a supercomputer. They calculated binding energies for drug models containing up to 12,635 atoms. The previous benchmark for this kind of calculation was only 303 atoms. Nvidia is also adding a quantum interface to Slurm supercomputer scheduling software. Today, each research centre must build its own custom setup to handle quantum tasks.

Scientists need faster decoders because quantum computers cannot grow without better classical computing power. Jerry Chow from IBM said scaling quantum and classical together will open new scientific frontiers.

This work could help set the rules for building future fault-tolerant quantum computers. Faster calculations may also help scientists discover new medicines and materials sooner. Listeners should keep in mind that the platform remains a proposal without set funding. We should watch to see when the companies announce an official start date.

Next, we look at global discussions about money and the environment.

Why are poor nations struggling to get climate money from wealthy countries? Rich nations are focusing on domestic costs and war, slowing down climate funding for vulnerable countries.

Two years ago, rich countries agreed to triple climate funding for poorer nations. They promised 300 billion dollars per year by 2035. They also set a goal of 1.3 trillion dollars annually from all sources combined. However, rich countries met their earlier 2020 climate funding target two years late. Since then, climate action has slipped down the political agenda for Western governments. United States President Donald Trump withdrew international funding and left the Paris Climate Agreement. In addition, wars in Ukraine and West Asia increased inflation and raised security costs. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimated world military spending reached 2.89 trillion dollars in 2025. That was up 2.9 percent in real terms from 2024.

Delegates from over 190 countries gathered in Antalya, Turkiye, for the COP31 climate conference.

Vulnerable small island nations reported that necessary repair cash is arriving far too slowly. Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale stated his country remains in a perpetual climate recovery mode. The Solomon Islands pledged 400,000 dollars of its own money to show leadership. The Bahamas committed 75 million dollars to protect seagrass meadows that store carbon. Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine appealed to delegates to find money for life, not death. Meanwhile, Britain used savings from climate grants to fund a cap on domestic bus fares. Analysis by Brazil showed climate finance reached 137 billion dollars in 2024. However, Brazil reported that funding could fall 840 billion dollars short of the annual goal. The United States did not send an official delegation to the summit for the second year. Outside the talks, over 10,000 protesters marched to demand urgent climate action and worker rights. Lala Peñaranda from Trade Unions for Energy Democracy called for energy to remain a public right. Turkish labor activist Kıvanç Eliaçık noted that Turkiye recently announced two new oil fields.

Host nation Turkiye and co-host Australia want to focus on making past pledges work. Australian negotiator Chris Bowen stated climate finance must become faster, simpler, and fairer.

HSBC sustainability officer Julian Wentzel said private investors need predictable costs before investing. Multilateral development banks reported record lending levels in 2025 according to the European Investment Bank. These banks have pledged to simplify application rules so money reaches poor nations faster. Listeners should watch whether rich nations increase grant commitments before the summit ends next week.

Now, we turn to a major failure in the private space launch business.

What caused a top space company to lose dozens of Amazon satellites during launch? A Vulcan rocket built by United Launch Alliance failed mid-flight, destroying all forty satellites on board.

Boeing and Lockheed Martin created United Launch Alliance in 2006 to build reliable rockets. Before this week, the company maintained a perfect 100 percent launch success record for two decades. Amazon hired the alliance to launch satellites for its new internet network, named Leo. Amazon has booked 38 flights on the Vulcan rocket to build its network. Amazon wants Leo to rival SpaceX's Starlink network, which operates more than 11,000 satellites. However, Amazon has faced severe delays getting its satellites into space. SpaceX builds its own rockets, but Amazon must buy launches from external providers. In May, a New Glenn rocket built by Blue Origin suffered an engine explosion on the launchpad. Amazon also booked 24 flights on that New Glenn rocket. The Vulcan rocket experienced earlier booster problems during a mission for the United States Space Force. Because of those earlier issues, the Pentagon had not yet approved Vulcan for national security missions.

On Sunday, a Vulcan rocket launched from Cape Canaveral in Florida carrying forty Amazon Leo satellites.

Roughly ten minutes after liftoff, the rocket suffered an anomaly and failed to reach orbit. The failure destroyed all forty Amazon satellites carried inside the rocket. This marked the very first mission failure for United Launch Alliance since its founding. The first-stage engines fired longer than expected before the stages separated. The anomaly then occurred after the hydrogen-powered Centaur upper stage engines began their planned burn. United Launch Alliance stated that every flight generates data and teaches engineers something new. Amazon stated it believes the launch alliance will learn from the failure and continue long-term plans. Currently, Amazon has deployed about 390 satellites, which is 12 percent of its planned target. The Federal Communications Commission requires Amazon to have 1,600 satellites in orbit by July 2026. Amazon ultimately aims to launch 3,232 satellites for complete global coverage by July 2029.

This launch was Vulcan's first flight in nine months following earlier safety investigations into its engines. The company was trying to establish a regular launch schedule for Amazon before this failure happened.

Engineers expect a lengthy investigation that could keep the Vulcan rocket grounded for several months. This grounding could deepen a broader launch bottleneck across the United States space industry. SpaceX is no longer taking new bookings for its Falcon 9 rocket, limiting options for satellite companies. Listeners should watch to see if Amazon can still meet its strict 2026 government deadline.

Up next, we examine questions from Scott Bessent about Nvidia's earnings and chip sales in China.

Did Nvidia use illegal chip sales to China to boost its profits? U.S. leaders are currently arguing over whether the government failed to stop improper chip sales.

Nvidia is the leading American company that designs advanced computer chips for artificial intelligence. These specialized chips help computers learn fast and run powerful smart programs. The United States government puts strict rules on exporting these high-tech chips to foreign countries. Officials set these trade controls to protect national security and keep America's technology advantage. But a Singapore technology company named Megaspeed came under investigation for violating these rules. Intelligence officials suspect Megaspeed helped move restricted Nvidia chips to buyers in China. Officials also suspect a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, has links to Beijing. Reports revealed former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had a personal relationship with Alice Huang. The Commerce Department maintains a trade blacklist called the Entity List. Placing a foreign company on this blacklist limits its access to American tech. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick controls which foreign companies get added to this list.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly criticized Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for delaying action against Megaspeed.

Bessent said several government agencies wanted to blacklist Megaspeed months ago. But he said the Commerce Department held the pen and failed to act. President Donald Trump addressed the rift between his two cabinet officials. Trump said Lutnick delayed restrictions to avoid escalating trade tensions with Beijing. Trump stated he understands both sides, and he ruled out firing Lutnick. Meanwhile, Senator Maria Cantwell sent a letter to Lutnick on Sunday. She alleged the department failed to stop China from accessing top American AI technology. Cantwell noted Lutnick's sons control a firm that held 1.2 billion dollars in Nvidia stock. Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott summoned both Lutnick and Jensen Huang to testify in December. Senator Elizabeth Warren and Senator Chris Coons instructed officials to preserve all documents about chip exports.

This political battle comes right before planned meetings between American officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Democrats will take control of Congress in January and plan to investigate these chip exports thoroughly. Tighter export enforcement could slow down chip sales for tech companies operating in Asia. But failing to enforce trade rules could allow foreign rivals to train advanced artificial intelligence. Watch to see if Congress pushes for stricter trade limits when Lutnick testifies next month.

Turning to our next story, energy shortages are creating serious challenges across the Middle East.

Why is Iran facing major natural gas shortages as winter begins? Recent military strikes by the United States and Israel damaged key energy processing plants.

Iran holds the second largest natural gas reserves in the whole world, right behind Russia. Natural gas is vital for Iran, making up 73 percent of its energy mix. Households rely on gas for home heating, while factories use it to power production. But Iran's energy system suffers from old equipment, poor storage capacity, and inefficient public consumption. Years of international sanctions restricted funding and made getting repair tools very hard. The situation worsened on February 28, when U.S. and Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Then on March 18, 26 projectiles struck six major gas processing refineries in Iran. That military attack knocked out 28 percent of Iran's gas production capacity right away. Workers restored about 100 million cubic meters per day of processing capacity since then. But government officials say fully restoring the remaining capacity could take until 2028.

Cold winter weather is now arriving, which causes household gas use to rise very quickly.

Iran's government forecasts a peak gas deficit of 430 million cubic meters per day this winter. That is much larger than last winter's deficit of 300 million cubic meters per day. Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani warned gas might be cut off across the entire country. She said 11 of Iran's 31 provinces face severe risks of heating cutoffs. The government ordered state offices to reduce their gas consumption by 20 percent. Offices must set thermostats to 64 degrees Fahrenheit and turn off heat on holidays. Inspections already led to gas cutoffs at six Tehran government buildings, including the Education Ministry. Zagros Petrochemical Company was forced to shut down a methanol production unit until further notice. To prevent power blackouts, power plants will burn heavy oil called mazut, which heavily pollutes air. Senior Iranian sources told reporters Iran is now in talks to import gas from Russia.

Temperatures are dropping quickly, while a naval blockade makes importing food and goods harder during war.

Iranian leaders fear gas shortages could trigger public unrest during an already severe economic crisis. High inflation and destroyed jobs have already made daily life very difficult for ordinary citizens. If factory gas gets shut off, more people could lose work and prices could rise. Watch to see if Iran can secure emergency natural gas imports from Russia before winter deepens.

Next, we look at how health policy leaders are navigating changing political control in Washington.

Why are medical school leaders staying cautious after Democrats won control of Congress? New political leaders might not automatically solve financial pressures and policy threats facing health organizations.

The Association of American Medical Colleges represents thousands of medical educators, doctors, and health researchers. Over the past two years, medical schools faced deep policy struggles during President Trump's second term. The administration considered reducing federal research funding through the National Institutes of Health. Officials also proposed cuts to Medicaid and costly visa restrictions for foreign medical workers. International medical graduates make up one quarter of all practicing doctors in the United States. These proposals threatened to place severe financial stress on teaching hospitals and medical schools. Medical leaders argued these changes would harm public health and stall important scientific discoveries. Then, Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in recent midterm elections.

Over four thousand medical school leaders gathered in Southern California for their annual conference to plan ahead.

Group official Danielle Turnipseed warned attendees that a Democrat-led Congress will not make their challenges disappear. Chief executive David Skorton said he remains concerned about how federal research grants get reviewed. Congress previously blocked the White House from putting grant reviews under direct political control. But that protective measure is set to expire on December 11. Skorton warned the administration might still attempt to change rules agency by agency. He also noted that Senator Susan Collins, a major Republican champion for research, lost her election. However, Skorton expressed optimism that research funding will keep receiving support from both political parties. He emphasized that medical groups must earn back public trust by being transparent about research spending.

Medical leaders are setting their strategy right as new lawmakers prepare to take office in Washington.

If federal rules change, political officials could gain more control over which scientific projects get funded. Tighter visa rules could also limit the number of foreign doctors entering American hospitals. That might lead to doctor shortages and longer wait times for patients seeking medical care. Watch to see if Congress extends the protection against political grant reviews before December 11.

Now, we turn to Europe, where British farmers hope a new UK-EU deal will revive post-Brexit trade.

British farmers want a new trade deal to lower border barriers with Europe. One farmer in Sussex hopes a proposed agreement between the United Kingdom and Europe may ease trade rules. Farmers across the country are pushing for these changes to make moving goods easier. A reporter from Al Jazeera spoke with the Sussex farmer about these trade barriers.

Moving on to news in the technology world.

Blackstone has acquired a majority stake in data center joint ventures with Amazon. The investment trust took a majority interest in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services. This deal focuses on data centers shared by the companies.

Next, let us look at global money markets.

Why is the United States dollar rising while Japan's economy shrinks? The American dollar reached its highest level in nineteen months because investors expect higher interest rates.

Currencies are the national money that people and businesses use every day. When a central bank raises interest rates, holding that country's currency earns more money. Because of those higher returns, investors around the world buy more of that currency. Central banks like the Federal Reserve in the United States set these rates to guide growth. If inflation rises too fast, central banks often raise rates to slow down spending. When economic growth slows down, central banks may pause rate hikes to help businesses. Over time, currency values change constantly as investors try to guess future central bank moves.

Last week, several Federal Reserve officials gave hawkish comments favoring higher rates. At the same time, new data showed United States inflation was hotter than expected. Because of those events, traders increased their bets on quicker interest rate hikes.

Today, the dollar index rose 0.1 percent to 103.52, its highest point in nineteen months. This was the fifth straight day of gains for the American greenback. Investors are waiting to hear comments from Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh. According to the CME Group FedWatch tool, traders see an 89.7 percent probability of a 25-basis-point hike. They also see a 10.3 percent chance of a larger 50-basis-point hike in December. Meanwhile, Japan reported that its economy contracted by an annualised 0.1 percent in the third quarter. That result was weaker than expected growth of 0.3 percent. Despite that soft data, the Japanese yen traded flat against the dollar at 159.59 yen. It was 0.1 percent stronger against the euro at 175.81 yen. Other currencies fell against the dollar. The euro dropped 0.1 percent to 1.1010 US dollars. The British pound fell 0.2 percent to 1.3189 US dollars. The Australian dollar fell 0.3 percent to 0.6751 US dollars. The kiwi dollar dropped 0.2 percent to 0.5516 US dollars. In crypto markets, Bitcoin fell 1.2 percent to 64,261 US dollars after a weekend drop. Ether dropped 1.3 percent to 1,794 US dollars.

This shift is happening right now because recent inflation data raised expectations for rate hikes. Markets are also pausing before big announcements from major technology companies later this week.

Francesco Pesole, an FX strategist at ING, said weak technology earnings could push the dollar down. He pointed to Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's market debut as key events to watch. Masahiko Loo, chief fixed-income strategist at State Street Investment Management, offered another view. He expects Japan's central bank to look past the soft economic data unless domestic wages drop. He also noted that government intervention risk rises if the yen weakens into the 160s. Listeners should watch upcoming Fed speeches and tech earnings for future currency moves.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Have you ever wondered why office chairs are almost always covered in rough, multi-colored fabric? You might think it was picked for soft comfort or modern style. However, it is actually a practical choice made by facilities managers. They use this synthetic fabric to keep offices looking clean over time. The mottled pattern with dark flecks is engineered to hide everyday wear and tear. It easily conceals everything from accidental coffee spills to tiny skin cells. By masking those spots, it prevents chairs from looking neglected. This saves money because chairs do not need to be replaced as often. Beyond hiding dirt, the dense weave serves another important purpose. It acts like an acoustic sponge across the entire office floor. The thick fabric absorbs ambient noise from the room. It also muffles creaking sounds when people shift in their seats. Without this material, a quiet office might sound like a hollow, echoing space. It is a chair designed to hide your mess and swallow your silence. Next time you sit down at your desk, notice the fabric beneath you. What other everyday items around you were designed to solve invisible problems?

Thank you for joining us on Sift In-Depth. Take a moment to enjoy the quiet, and we will talk again soon.
